attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own post, stated in his voice.

semantics.note: Keeps 'at this point' and 'entirely'. 'Driven by' is a causal claim. The later softening to 'largely (if not entirely)' is correctly flagged in the contract.

contract.note: Reading 'expansion' as new contracted demand and capacity, and 'entirely' as all or nearly all, is an ordinary plain reading. The result depends on treating backlog growth as the main measure, because who the capacity serves is not disclosed.

evidence.note: Company Q1 2025 release. Backlog grew from $15.1B to $25.9B. The OpenAI deal added $11.2B, while non-OpenAI RPO dipped slightly. Any new non-OpenAI bookings net of recognized revenue look small, so nearly all new contracted demand was OpenAI.
The CEO mentions 'other customer wins' and the W&B acquisition, but gives no sizes. Nothing here shows substantial non-OpenAI expansion, so it does not meet the contradiction condition.
Secondary summary of 2024 S-1 figures from before the target period. It supplies the $15.1B RPO baseline and shows other customers existed.

reviews.rationale: In Q1 2025 the OpenAI deal accounted for essentially all of CoreWeave's backlog growth, while other contracted demand was flat or slightly down. Other wins such as IBM are not shown to be substantial. Who the capacity buildout serves, and Microsoft's OpenAI share, are undisclosed. That leaves the capacity part unconfirmed but not contradicted. On the contract's plain reading of 'all or nearly all', the claim holds.

attribution.note: Zitron's own statement of belief in his own post.

semantics.note: 'I don't believe... any other viable options' is a firm denial, not a graded hedge like 'I suspect', so it is a factual observation about the time of the post. 'Existing' is preserved.

contract.note: 'Any other viable options' plainly means any workable supplier, not one that alone meets all of OpenAI's needs, so the contract reading is fair. Counting a deal finalized weeks later is a flagged choice, but Reuters says it was in talks for months before the post.

evidence.note: Reuters: Google Cloud agreed in May 2025, after months of talks, to supply additional capacity to OpenAI's existing infrastructure. This is a non-Microsoft option within the target period.
Google itself was capacity-constrained, so how much it could add is unclear. This bears on scale, not on whether the option existed.
July 2025 OpenAI supplier list names Google, Oracle and CoreWeave. Just after the target period; it corroborates e1.
2024 Oracle capacity was provided as an extension of Azure. It is ambiguous whether that counts as outside Microsoft.

reviews.rationale: Reuters reports that OpenAI arranged additional existing compute from Google Cloud, finalized in May 2025 after months of talks. That makes Google a viable non-Microsoft option around the time of the post. The size of Google's capacity is unknown and Google was constrained, but the claim denied that any such option existed, so it is contradicted.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: The antecedent is kept and 'will' is firm. The 'does not have much room to expand' clause is present tense in the source, and folding it into the forecast is a minor liberty.

contract.note: No rate was stated. Using the Aug 2024 to Mar 2025 average is reasonable, and the faster spike rate is flagged. Testing 'room to expand' against compute actually added in 2025 is a fair, ordinary reading.

evidence.note: Users went from 500M at end of March to 800M by Oct 2025, about 48M a month, at or above the baseline. The antecedent was met.
Sets the baseline: 200M in Aug 2024 and 400M in Feb 2025, giving about 43M a month to end of March.
Aug 2025: Altman cites capacity tradeoffs and compute prioritization. This bears out the capacity-issues part.
Reuters reporting the OpenAI CFO: compute rose from 0.6 GW to 1.9 GW in 2025, roughly tripling. This is a company disclosure, but it meets the contract's doubling test for room to expand.

reviews.rationale: Growth kept roughly the earlier pace, so the antecedent was met. The capacity-issues part held: in Aug 2025 OpenAI publicly cited capacity tradeoffs and rate limits. The room-to-expand part failed: OpenAI reported compute roughly tripling in 2025, from 0.6 to 1.9 GW. Both early-resolution events are dated before the evaluation date.
